analysis.one_liner: Caps out-of-pocket prescription drug costs at $2,000 a year in ACA marketplace plans.
analysis.headline: A single House Democrat introduced the bill with no cosponsors; it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee and has seen no action since.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would change the Affordable Care Act to put a hard annual limit on what people pay out of pocket for prescription drugs in plans bought on the ACA marketplaces: $2,000 a year for an individual, twice that for a family, starting in 2027 and rising with premiums afterward. Today those plans have an overall out-of-pocket maximum that can run several thousand dollars higher, and drug costs count toward it, so patients with expensive prescriptions can still owe a lot before the cap. This bill would make the drug limit much lower and separate.
analysis.who_benefits: People who buy their health coverage through the ACA marketplaces and take expensive prescriptions. Under current law they can owe thousands of dollars in drug cost-sharing before hitting the plan's overall limit; this bill would cut that drug-specific exposure to $2,000 a year for an individual. Everyone with marketplace coverage benefits indirectly if fewer people abandon prescriptions they cannot afford, which can prevent costlier medical crises later.

how_it_helps.text: The bill writes a drug-specific cost-sharing ceiling into the ACA: annual out-of-pocket spending on prescription drugs cannot exceed $2,000 for self-only coverage beginning in plan year 2027, and twice that ($4,000) for other coverage tiers [S2].
The $2,000 cap rises each year after 2027 by the ACA's premium adjustment percentage, rounded down to the nearest $50, so the protection is permanent rather than a one-year fix [S2].
The bill also amends the ACA's preventive-services and essential-health-benefits provisions so plans must honor the new drug limit as part of required cost-sharing rules [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers offering marketplace plans would owe the difference whenever a patient's drug cost-sharing would otherwise exceed $2,000, and they would likely pass part of that cost back to all enrollees through higher premiums. Brand-name drug makers would not pay anything under the bill; the prices of their drugs are untouched, so the money simply moves from patients to insurers rather than shrinking. People with employer plans, Medicare, or Medicaid get no direct benefit from this bill.

drawbacks.text: The bill does not lower the underlying price of any drug; it only shifts who pays. If insurers absorb more drug cost-sharing, they can raise premiums for everyone with marketplace coverage, so some people who use few or no prescriptions would pay more [S2].
It covers only ACA marketplace plans. People with employer-sponsored insurance, Medicare, or Medicaid get no new protection, so a large share of Americans with high drug costs is left out [S2].

A separate drug cap can make the total burden confusing: patients would still owe other medical cost-sharing up to the plan's overall out-of-pocket maximum, on top of what they pay toward premiums [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For marketplace enrollees with serious prescription needs, the benefit is real and large: a guaranteed $2,000 ceiling instead of a bill that can run several times that. The cost is diffuse — somewhat higher premiums spread across all marketplace customers — and the bill leaves drug prices themselves untouched, so it treats a symptom rather than the cause. It is also narrow: it helps only the marketplace population, not people with employer or Medicare coverage who face the same problem. On balance it is a genuine but partial fix.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, where it has sat with no cosponsors and no scheduled action since day one.

narrative.text: Rep. Jake Auchincloss (D-MA) introduced the bill on November 20, 2025 [S1][S4].
It was referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, which holds jurisdiction over ACA market regulation [S4].
No other member of the House has cosponsored the bill — the cosponsor count is zero [S3].
The committee has taken no further action: no markup, no vote, and no floor consideration appear in the action history [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far the outcome is simply the status quo. Insurers and drug makers keep the existing cost-sharing structure — patients with expensive prescriptions can still owe thousands out of pocket — because the bill has not moved an inch.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Status quo; insurers and drug makers unaffected so far

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Rep. Brett Guthrie (R-KY)
against.what_they_did: Has taken no action on the bill since it was referred — no markup, no vote, no scheduling

sides.party_line_note: No party-line split is visible because the bill has exactly one sponsor, a House Democrat, and zero cosponsors from either party [S3].

industries.industry: Health insurers selling ACA marketplace plans
industries.note: Insurers would owe the gap between actual drug cost-sharing and the $2,000 cap, but can recoup it through premiums on all marketplace customers. Patients with big prescriptions win; enrollees who use no drugs may pay more.

The bill leaves drug list prices untouched, so manufacturers keep full revenue while insurers and patients' premiums cover more of the bill. Cheaper prescriptions may also mean more filled prescriptions and more volume.
The bill regulates only patient cost-sharing, not rebate or pricing practices, so PBMs' role in setting effective drug costs is unchanged and their negotiating leverage stays intact.

analysis.trajectory: With a single sponsor, zero cosponsors, and referral to a committee run by the opposing party, the bill is unlikely to receive a markup or a floor vote this Congress. Most bills in this position die quietly at the end of the session; movement would require either attracting cosponsors across the aisle or leadership deciding to prioritize it.
